reasons: The servants are puzzled. "Didn't you sow good seed in your field?" only leads into their real question, "Where then did the weeds come from?", and the owner answers it. It is not plainly a question asked for force, and the span also starts on a stray comma.
"What do you think, Simon?" really asks for Peter's view, and Peter answers in 17:26 ("From others"). It is not a question that tells. The span also leaves out "What".

The astonished disciples' "Who then can be saved?" may be a real cry of perplexity, and Jesus answers it in 19:26. It is not plainly a question that tells, and when in doubt the place does not go live.
"But what do you think?" introduces the parable of the two sons and asks for a judgment that the hearers later give (21:31). It is not a question that tells, and the span also leaves out "what".
"What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?" is a real question, and the Pharisees answer it ("David's"). The question that tells comes later, in 22:43-45. The span also leaves out "What".
The high priest's "What do you think?" calls for a verdict, and the council gives one ("He deserves to die"). It is a real question, not one that tells, and the span also leaves out "What".

"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" is a cry of anguish to God from the cross. The verse does not plainly show it is asked only to make a point and not as a real lament, so in doubt it stays out.
"Overwhelmed with fear", the disciples ask one another "Who is this...?" It reads as real, awed wondering about who He is. It is not plainly a question asked only to make a point.

"And how can He perform such miracles?" comes from people who "were astonished". On its own it may be real puzzlement. The scorn only shows in 6:3 ("Isn't this the carpenter...?", "they took offense"), so in doubt this one stays out.

"Who then can be saved?" carries dismay, but Jesus answers it as a real question in 10:27 ("With man this is impossible, but not with God"). It is not plainly a question that is not asking. The readers split, so in doubt it stays out.

"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" is a cry of anguish from the cross. Nothing in the verse plainly shows it is asked only to make a point rather than as a true lament. Same judgment as Matthew 27:46.

"Child, why have You done this to us?" carries reproach, but it is also a real question from anxious parents, and Jesus gives a reason in reply (2:49). It is not plainly a question that is not asking.

The guests say 'Who is this who even forgives sins?' to themselves. It can be read as offence, but just as well as real wonder about who Jesus is (compare 8:25). The verse does not settle which, so it is not plain enough to go live unnamed.

Jesus asks for the lawyer's judgment and gets an answer in 10:37 ('The one who showed him mercy'). That makes it a real, leading question, not plainly one that does not ask. The span also cut off 'Which of these three'.

"Those who heard this asked, 'Who then can be saved?'" reads as a real question put to Jesus, and He answers it in 18:27 ("What is impossible with man is possible with God"). It is not plainly a question that tells.

"How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?" voices surprise. It can still fairly be read as a real question about why He asks her, and Jesus answers her in 4:10. Since we are in doubt, it is not plain enough to go live.

"So the disciples asked one another, 'Could someone have brought Him food?'" is a real, puzzled question after "I have food to eat that you know nothing about", and Jesus explains in 4:34. It makes no point of its own.
"Woman, where are your accusers?" draws a real answer from her, "No one, Lord" (8:11), and leads on to "neither do I condemn you". It works as dialogue, so it is not plainly a question that tells.
The neighbors really were asking who he was. In 9:9 they are unsure: "Some claimed that he was, but others said, 'No, he just looks like him.'" It is a real question, not a figure.
The people were "asking one another", "What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?" These are real questions seeking opinions, not a figure. The marked words also cut off "What".
Thomas's "how can we know the way?" comes from real confusion, and Jesus answers it in 14:6 ("I am the way"). It can be read as a real request, so the figure is not plain.

"Didn't I see you with Him in the garden?" is an accusing question that waits for an answer, and Peter gives one by denying it (18:27), as with the question in 18:25. It is not plainly a question that asks nothing.

"What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew?" is raised to be answered at once ("Much in every way", 3:2). The point is made by the answer, and the answer the question seems to suggest (none) is the opposite of Paul's, so it is not plainly a question that tells.

"That God is unjust to inflict His wrath on us?" voices an objection that 3:6 answers ("Certainly not!"). That is question and answer, and so in doubt as a question that tells. The span is also the whole verse, and the tags sit on the if-clause.
"What then? Are we any better? Not at all." is question and answer, and the point is in the answer. The span runs through the whole verse, and the tags mark only Τί οὖν.

"Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not!" raises an objection in order to answer it, and the point is in the answer. The span also takes in "Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law."
"What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather, has discovered?" opens a question that 4:2-3 answer. It makes no point of its own.
"For what does the Scripture say?" only introduces the quotation that answers it, and the span also takes in that quotation.

"Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised?" is an open question that Paul works out in 4:10-12, not one whose answer is plain from the question. The span also takes in the next sentence.
"Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before." is question and answer in one verse, so the point is in the answer, and the span includes that answer.

"Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?" voices an objection that 6:2 answers ("Certainly not!"). That is question and answer, and so in doubt as a question that tells. The tags mark only the formula Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν.

"Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!" is an objection answered at once, so the point is in the answer. The marked words begin with a stray "?", and the tags mark only Τί οὖν, which lies outside the marked words.
"What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not!" is objection and answer, so the point is in the answer. The marked words are the whole verse, and the tags mark only Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν.
"Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not!" raises an objection in order to answer it, and the point is in the answer. The span also runs through the whole answer.

"Is God unjust? Certainly not!" raises an objection and then answers it. The point is made by "Certainly not!", not by the question, so this is question-and-answer, which is not a live form, and not a question that tells on its own. Doubt means drop. The marked words also begin with a stray "? ", and the tags mark Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν, which is outside the marked words.

This verse is the middle of one unfinished sentence that runs from 9:22 to 9:24. The BSB supplies "What if", and the verse ends in a dash. In the Greek, καὶ ἵνα γνωρίσῃ is a purpose clause with no question word, so the claim that the figure shows only in the original is backwards. The figure is not plain at these words, and the tags are just the first eight words.

"What then will we say?" only leads into Paul's own conclusion, which he then states outright ("That the Gentiles ... have obtained it"). It is a question answered at once, not a question that tells, and the marked words take in the answer as well. No live form fits.
"Why not?" only sets up Paul's own answer ("Because their pursuit was not by faith"). The question itself tells nothing, so the figure is not plain.
"'Who will descend into the Abyss?'" is a question Paul tells the reader not to say in his heart. Whether it is a real question or one that tells needs interpreting, so it is not plain.
"But what does it say?" only leads into the quotation that answers it and makes no point of its own. The marked words also take in the whole verse.
"And what was the divine reply to him?" only leads into the quoted answer and makes no point of its own. The marked words also take in the whole answer.
"What then?" is a bare link to the next point, which Paul gives at once. The question tells nothing, and the span covers the whole verse.

The BSB has an exclamation, "how much greater riches will their fullness bring!", not a question. The Greek question mark was added by an editor to a how-much-more argument, so the figure is not plain. The tags fall on the if-clause.

The BSB ends with an exclamation, "how much more readily will these... be grafted into their own olive tree!". It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and the Greek question mark is an editor's. The tags fall on the if-clause.

"Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right" uses the question as an if-clause, and the command answers it. It is not plainly a question that tells. The tags fall on "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct".

"What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?" are questions Paul answers at once ("They are servants..."). The answer makes the point, not the question, so the figure is not plain. The span also takes in the answer.

"Was a man already circumcised when he was called?" stands for "if a man was", and a command answers it. It states a case and is not plainly a question that tells. The span also takes in the commands.

"Were you a slave when you were called?" stands for "if you were a slave", and the instruction answers it. It states a case and is not plainly a question that tells. The span also takes in the instruction.

"Are you committed to a wife?" works as an "if" (if you are bound, do not seek release). It does not make a point the way a question that tells does. The span also takes in both commands, and the tags miss λέλυσαι.

The question opens in 11:14 ("Doesn't nature itself teach you..."). This verse holds only its tail plus a plain statement, "For long hair is given to her as a covering", so the figure is not at these words.

These are questions Paul puts in an objector's mouth so that he can answer them at length (15:36 onward). Paul treats them as real questions, so the verse does not plainly show questions that are not asking, and when in doubt a place does not go live. The marked words and tags also take in "But someone will ask" (Ἀλλ᾽ ἐρεῖ τις), which is not part of any question.

The questions are plainly not asking, but the tags (G5101, G0770G, G2532, G3756, G0770G) are exactly the five words of the first question, "Who is weak, and I am not weak?". The marked English also takes in "Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?", whose own words (G4624, G1473, G4448) are untagged, and "and" is tagged twice. The tags do not match the marked words.

The two questions in "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?" are plainly rhetorical. But the tags (G5101, G0770G, G2532, G3756, G0770G) were taken from the first question only. The second question's own words, σκανδαλίζεται "is led into sin" and πυροῦμαι "burn", are untagged, while its τίς, καί and οὐκ are highlighted. So the Greek highlight does not match the marked words.
The BSB verse is a statement with no question in it. The only sign of one is an editors' question mark in the Greek, and no other form shows plainly at the marked words.
The BSB gives an exclamation ending in "!", not a question. The question rests only on the editors' ";" in the Greek, so the figure is not plain to a reader of the BSB. When in doubt, it stays out.
The BSB reads "You see that his faith was working with his actions...", a plain statement. The question rests only on the editors' ";" in the Greek, so the figure is not plain.

"Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it..." uses the question as a way of saying "whoever is wise" to lead into a command. It does not plainly make a point of its own, so it stays out.

"Is any one of you suffering? He should pray." uses the question to mean "if anyone is suffering" and introduces an instruction, so it is not plainly a question that makes a point. The marked words also take in the commands.
As in 5:13, "Is any one of you sick?" stands for "if anyone is sick" and introduces an instruction, so it is not plainly a question that tells. The marked words also cover the whole command.

The question "Who then overcomes the world?" is rhetorical, but the marked words also take in the answer, "Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God." That answer is a plain statement, not part of the question, so the span is wrong. The other places in this batch that ask and answer mark only the question.

The question "Who then overcomes the world?" is rhetorical, but the marked span also takes in the answer, "Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God." Those words are not the question, so the span is too wide; elsewhere (Galatians 3:21, Luke 12:51) the answer is left out.

"Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?" is a herald's real summons. 5:3 says no one was found, and 5:5 names the Lamb, so it is not plainly a question asked without seeking an answer. The span and the tags also take in the narrative "And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice".

"How long, O Lord ... until You avenge our blood...?" is a plea that gets a real answer in 6:11 ("rest a little while longer, until..."), so the verse does not plainly show a question that is not asking. When in doubt it does not go live. The tags are mostly on the narrative frame kai ekraxan phone megale legontes.

"These in white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?" is a question in a dialogue put to John, who replies "Sir, you know", and the elder then answers in 7:14. It is not plainly a question that only makes a point. The span and the tags also take in the narrative "Then one of the elders addressed me".

The marked BSB words "Sarah had passed the age of childbearing" are a plain statement, not a gentle word. The gentle phrase is only in the Hebrew ("a way like the women"), and a BSB reader would not see a euphemism in the lit words. When in doubt, drop.

"he breathed his last and died ... and was gathered to his people": the verse already says plainly that he died, so the phrase does not stand in for a hard word. Whether it speaks gently of death, of burial, or of joining the dead takes a commentary to decide, so it is not plain enough to go live.

"Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people": the verse names death outright first, so the phrase does not take the place of a hard word. Calling it a euphemism needs interpretation.

In the BSB, "for I am having my period" is just the ordinary plain way to say it, so a reader would not see a gentle word standing in for a hard one. The gentle phrase is only in the Hebrew "[the] way of women", and the BSB words marked to carry it also take in "I am having". Since it is in doubt whether a reader of the marked words would see the figure without being told, it does not go live.

"Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people": the death is stated outright, so the phrase does not replace a hard word. Reading it as a euphemism rather than as burial or joining the dead takes a commentary.

The verse already names the death plainly ("breathed his last"), and then "he was gathered to his people" is said beside it, so the phrase does not take the place of a harder word. He is not buried until chapter 50, so it may say more than death. When in doubt, drop.

In "he will not dishonor his father's marriage bed" the bed stands for the marriage (closer to one thing named for another), and the verse already says "not to marry his father's wife"; a reader would not plainly see a gentle word here. When in doubt, drop.

The verse says the hard word outright: "you will die and be gathered to your people". So "be gathered to your people" is set beside "die" and does not stand in for it. It is not plainly a gentle word in place of a harsh one, and when in doubt the place does not go live.

"Asa died and rested with his fathers": the hard word "died" is said outright in the same clause, so "rested with his fathers" does not stand in for it. It is not plainly a gentle word in place of a hard one.

"lest I sleep in death" names death outright inside the marked words, so no gentle word hides the hard thing. Death likened to sleep might be read as a metaphor, but that is not plain enough to go live without a writer.

"It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence": line 1 already says "the dead" plainly, so line 2 softens nothing. "Silence" for the grave is at most a metonymy that is not plain enough to go live unnamed.
The gentle word the search means is in Hebrew not shown here; the BSB "You prostituted yourself with your lustful neighbors" is blunt, and the whole verse is marked.

"The girl is not dead, but asleep" denies death outright and sets sleep against it, so it is not plainly a gentler word put in place of a hard one; what the saying means needs explaining. When in doubt, drop.
"The child is not dead, but asleep" sets sleep against death and denies death, rather than plainly putting a gentle word in its place; how it works needs explaining. When in doubt, drop.
"she is not dead but asleep", answered by "knowing that she was dead" (8:53), denies death rather than plainly giving a gentle word for it; it needs interpreting. When in doubt, drop.

The figure is plain: with "the dead will be raised imperishable" in 15:52, "sleep" is clearly a gentle word for death. But only "sleep" carries it. The marked words "We will not all sleep" are a clause that contains the word, and "We will not all" adds nothing to the euphemism. The span should be "sleep", and when in doubt the place fails.

"away from the body and at home with the Lord" carries on the picture of the body as a dwelling (5:1, 5:6) and reads as a plain statement of what death brings, not plainly a gentle word for a hard thing.
Just before, in 5:6-7, "sleep" and "awake" mean moral slackness and watchfulness, so it is not plain from the verse that "asleep" here means dead.

"in his own likeness, after his own image" is two near-synonym phrases with no "and" joining two words into one thing, so hendiadys is not what the verse shows, and the prose offers no live form instead.
A BSB reader of "doing what is right and just" sees two related qualities; that they name one thing is an interpreter's reading, not plain in the verse.

The BSB reads "she quickly lowered her jar", so no two words joined by "and" are left to see. The Hebrew "she hurried and she put down" is ordinary narration, and calling it one thing named by two words takes a grammar to point it out.
"And she quickly emptied her jar" shows no pair joined by "and". The Hebrew "she hurried and she emptied" reads as two plain acts, so a reader would not see the figure without being told.

"She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder" has no pair joined by "and" in the BSB. The Hebrew "she hurried and she put down" is ordinary storytelling, not a plain case of two words for one thing.
"show kindness and faithfulness to my master" reads in the BSB as two qualities; that they are one thing is not plain without a commentary, and no Hebrew is shown.
No Hebrew words are shown here, and the BSB's "each one quickly lowered his sack" has no two words joined by "and", so a reader cannot see the figure.
"Now return quickly to my father" has no pair joined by "and". The Hebrew "hurry and go up" is a plain urgent command, and reading it as one idea named by two words needs a grammar to say so.
No Hebrew is shown, and in the BSB's "bring my father down here quickly" no two words are joined by "and". The figure cannot be seen in these words.
"promise to show me kindness and faithfulness" reads in the BSB as two qualities; that they are one thing is not plain from the verse, and no Hebrew is shown.
"to give them glory and splendor" pairs two near-synonyms, but nothing in the verse plainly shows one idea rather than two words heaped up.

The Hebrew 'and he hurried, Moses, and he bowed low' is one act, and the BSB gives it as 'immediately bowed down'. But the figure shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags include H4872 (Moses), which is not part of it. This step cannot cut the tags down to the two verbs. Without the tags, 'immediately bowed down' shows a BSB reader no two words joined by 'and'. So it does not go live.

The BSB has one phrase, "His covenant of loving devotion". The Hebrew "the covenant and the loyalty" could just as well name two things God keeps, so seeing one thing there is a reading only some would make.

The BSB keeps the two apart: 'keep His covenant and the loving devotion that He swore'. Nothing in the verse shows they are one thing. The marked words ('the', 'the loving devotion that He swore') leave out 'covenant', and three tags sit on the object marker H0853.
In the BSB, 'show you kindness and faithfulness' names two qualities. Reading them as one ('faithful kindness') takes a commentary; the verse does not show it. The span also takes in 'show you'.

The Hebrew 'and they hurried, the people, and they passed over' is one act, and the BSB gives it as 'The people hurried across'. But the tag H5971A (people) is not part of the figure, and it also marks the earlier 'to the people'. This step cannot cut the tags to the two verbs. Without them, the BSB words alone do not show two words joined by 'and'.

Three Hebrew verbs ('hurried', 'rose early', 'went out') become 'he hurried out early in the morning'. The main verb (H3318G, 'went out') is not tagged. The tagged pair alone is not a plain two-word figure, and the split spans 'he hurried' and 'early in the morning' do not mark one. In doubt, it does not go live.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "immediately set it on fire" has no two words joined by "and". A reader of the BSB would not see two words naming one thing.

The Hebrew 'and she made haste, the woman, and she ran' is given by the BSB as 'ran quickly'. But the tag H0802G (the woman) is not part of the figure, and the spans 'husband' and 'Behold' have nothing to do with it. This step cannot cut the tags to the two verbs. Without them, 'ran quickly' shows a BSB reader no two words joined by 'and'.
"So the man hurried over and reported to Eli" is plain narration. The Hebrew "he hurried and he came" is two ordinary acts, not a plain case of two words for one thing.

The Hebrew 'and he hurried, David, and he ran' is given by the BSB as 'David ran quickly'. But the tag H1732 (David) is not part of the figure and marks both Davids in the verse, and the span 'him' is stray. This step cannot cut the tags to the two verbs. Without them, 'ran quickly' alone does not show the figure.
The BSB reads "Come quickly", with no pair joined by "and". The Hebrew "make haste and come" is an ordinary urgent command, and a reader would not see the figure without being told.

The tag H0026G (Abigail) is not part of the figure, and the span takes in 'Then Abigail'. This step cannot cut the tags to the two verbs. Without the Hebrew, the BSB's 'hurried and took two hundred loaves' reads as two acts, so the BSB words alone do not show one idea.
"she quickly got off the donkey" has no pair joined by "and" in the BSB. The Hebrew "she made haste and she came down" reads as ordinary narration.
"if you had not come quickly to meet me" shows no two words joined by "and". The Hebrew "you had made haste and you had come" is ordinary speech, so the figure is not plain.

The tags H4116A and H6965B ('made haste', 'arose') are right, but the BSB does not make them one act. It keeps 'hurried and got on a donkey', where 'got on' renders 'rode' and 'arose' is not rendered at all. The single marked word 'hurried' cannot carry a two-word figure, and the BSB does not back it up as it does where it writes 'quickly'. In doubt, it does not go live.

The Hebrew 'and he made haste, Saul, and he fell' is given by the BSB as 'Immediately Saul fell'. But the tag H7586G (Saul) is not part of the figure, and the span runs Saul into it. This step cannot cut the tags to the two verbs. Without them, the BSB words alone show no two words joined by 'and'.
"and she quickly slaughtered it" shows no pair joined by "and" in the BSB. The Hebrew "she made haste and she slaughtered it" reads as two plain acts in a run of acts (took, kneaded, baked).
In the BSB, 'show you loving devotion and faithfulness' names two qualities. Nothing in the verse shows they are one thing. The span also takes in 'show you'.
'administered justice and righteousness' reads in the BSB as two things David did. Reading them as one idea comes from an interpreter, not from the verse. The span also takes in 'administered'.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "he will soon overtake us" has no two words joined by "and". The figure cannot be seen here.
In the BSB, 'May the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness' names two qualities. Nothing in the verse shows them as one thing. The span also takes in 'show you'.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "Your covenant of loving devotion" joins no two words with "and". Without the original words a reader would not see two words naming one thing.
'to carry out justice and righteousness' reads in the BSB as two things. Nothing in the verse shows them as one idea. The span also takes in 'carry out'.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "the prophet quickly removed the bandage" has no two words joined by "and". The figure cannot be seen in these words.
"Quickly, each man took his garment" has no pair joined by "and" in the BSB. The Hebrew "they hurried and they took" is ordinary narration, not a plain case of two words for one thing.

In the BSB, 'ascribe to the LORD glory and strength' names two things to ascribe, and the next verse speaks of 'the glory due His name' on its own. Nothing shows them as one. The span also takes in 'ascribe to the LORD'.
'administered justice and righteousness' reads in the BSB as two things. The one-idea reading needs a commentary. The span also takes in 'administered'.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "Your covenant of loving devotion" joins no two words with "and". A BSB reader would not see the figure.
'to carry out justice and righteousness' reads in the BSB as two things. Nothing in the verse shows them as one. The span also takes in 'carry out'.
No Hebrew is shown, and the BSB's "His covenant of loving devotion" has no two words joined by "and". The figure is not visible without the original words.
The BSB has one phrase, "who keeps His gracious covenant". The Hebrew "the covenant and the loyalty" could name two things God keeps, so seeing one thing there is a reading only some would make.

'May darkness and gloom reclaim it' heaps up two words for darkness, as the next lines heap 'a cloud' and 'the blackness of the day'. Neither the Hebrew nor the BSB shows one word qualifying the other to name a single thing. The span also takes in 'May'.

The span is the whole verse. The BSB's 'I heard a whispering voice' has no pair joined by 'and'. The 'silence and a voice' reading comes from a commentator cited in the search's note, and no Hebrew is shown.

In "You crowned him with glory and honor" a BSB reader sees two gifts named. Nothing in the verse shows them meaning one thing, so the reading depends on a commentary. The marked words also take in "crowned him with".

"ascribe to the LORD glory and strength" names two things, and verse 2 goes on with "the glory due His name" alone. The verse does not plainly make them one, and the marked words also take in the verb.

"You have exercised justice / and righteousness in Jacob" sits beside "loves justice" and "established equity" and reads as a list of qualities, not one thing. The marked words also cross the BSB's line break and take in "exercised".
"The LORD executes righteousness / and justice for all the oppressed" names two things over two BSB lines. Nothing in the verse shows them as one idea, and the marked words also take in "executes".

"sat in darkness and in the shadow of death" repeats "in" and piles up two words for gloom. Nothing in the verse plainly makes one qualify the other. The two marked spans overlap and duplicate each other.
"out of darkness and the shadow of death" pairs two words for gloom, and nothing in the verse plainly shows them as one thing. The two marked spans overlap and duplicate each other.
"I have done what is just and right" reads as two near-synonym qualities. The verse does not plainly show two words naming one thing, and the marked words also take in "done what is".
"To do righteousness and justice" names two things in the BSB. Reading them as one idea is an interpreter's view and is not plain in the verse. The marked words also take in "To do".

The whole verse is marked, and the BSB has no pair joined by "and": "share a house with a quarrelsome wife" already merges the Hebrew. Any hendiadys is only in the Hebrew, which is not shown and has no tags, so the verse does not plainly show it.
"a right time and procedure to every purpose" reads just as naturally as two things, the time and the way. Seeing one idea in it takes a commentator.

All four lines are marked, not a pair. The only possible pair, "by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire", repeats "spirit" and can be read as two descriptions. Reading it as one burning spirit of judgment is a commentator's reading.
All six lines are marked. The only pair, "with plenty of fire and wood", reads plainly as two things on the pyre, fuel and flame. "Wood fire" is Delitzsch's reading, not something the verse shows.

The tags rightly mark the two verbs, "and they may hasten" and "and they may take up". But after 9:17's "summon the wailing women; send for the most skillful", hastening reads naturally as their coming, which is how the BSB renders it ("come quickly and take up"). It may be two acts, so one act in two verbs is not plain.

"administer justice and righteousness in the land" reads plainly as two qualities of the King's rule. Calling the pair one idea is a scholar's reading, and the span also takes in the verb "administer".

"He will administer justice / and righteousness in the land" is the same stock pair as 23:5, and it reads as two qualities. Nothing shows they are one idea. The span also runs across two BSB lines and takes in the verb.
"does what is just and right" joins two near-synonyms that a reader takes as two qualities of his conduct. One idea in two words is not plain, and the span takes in "does what is".
"has done what is just and right" is the same ordinary pair as 18:5. Nothing in the verse shows one idea, and the span includes the verb.
In "keeps all My statutes, and does what is just and right", the pair reads as two qualities, so the figure is not plain. The span includes the verb.
"does what is just and right, he will save his life" uses the same stock pair of near-synonyms, which is not plainly one idea. The span includes the verb.
In "turns from his sin and does what is just and right", the pair is not plainly one idea without a commentary, and the span includes the verb.
"He has done what is just and right" is the same stock pair, which a reader takes as two qualities. The span includes "done what is".
